standard.clear: Explicit adverse judgment of the leader or explicitly attributed conduct, including personal sovereignty-denying nicknames; shared explicit blame remains eligible.

source_context.text: European Union/Canada

Q. Mr. President, you've talked about the VAT and the EU before, and your—your concerns with how the EU treats you. Do you have a number in mind—of the European Union, do you have an idea where that number is going to land?
The President. Well, what they are now is they have a 20-percent VAT tax, which we're considering to be similar or the same as the tariff, plus they charge lots of fees.

And, you know, they're doing something else. European Union has been very tough on our companies. They sued Apple. They sued Google. They sued Facebook. They sued many other companies. And they're American companies, and the kind of numbers are staggering.

And the court system over there is not very good to our companies. If you know that Apple had to pay, I think, $16 billion in a penalty—a court case that was really shocking, because most people thought they would have won that court case—people that watched it. So they've been very tough.

Airlines have called me up, and they said, "Could you help us with Europe because they're charging us so many different fees?" I got a call from the head of American, United, and other airlines saying, "Every time we land a plane, we get just absolutely killed by the European Union." And so they haven't been—treated us good.
You know, we think European Union is wonderful. We all love Europe. We love our—the countries in Europe, but European Union has been absolutely brutal on trade.

Canada has been very bad to us on trade, but now Canada is going to have to start paying up. And Canada has been tough on the military because they don't have a very—they have a very low military cost. They think we're going to, you know, protect them with our military, which is unfair.
So Canada is going to be a very interesting situation, because, you know, we just don't need their product, and yet, they survive off the fact that we're—you know, we do 95 percent of what they do.

And Canada is just absolutely—I say it and sometimes people smile and sometimes they say, "Great idea"—but Canada would—their taxes would come down greatly, their security would go up greatly. Amazing things happen to Canada.

And really, Canada, in this particular—why would we pay $200 billion a year in subsidies to Canada when they're not a State? You do that for a State, but you don't do that for somebody else's country. So I think Canada is going to be a very serious contender to be our 51st State.

Q. A number of industries have come to you asking for exemptions on tariffs. Is that something that is under consideration by you?

The President. Well, people are coming to me and talking about tariffs, and a lot of people are asking me if they could have exceptions. And once you do that for one, you have to do that for all. So, I mean, generally—I did something interestingly during—2 weeks ago. I gave the American car companies a break because it would have been unfair if I didn't. And everybody said, "Oh, he changed his mind on tariffs." I didn't change my mind. I helped our, you know, sort of Big Three, Big Four. I helped some of the American companies. So there'll be flexibility. But basically, it's reciprocal so that if China is charging us 50 percent or 30 percent or 20 percent—and I don't mean China. I mean anybody, any country— Canada.

Nobody knows that Canada is charging our dairy farmers—they have 270-percent tariffs. Nobody knows that. Nobody knows that. They have up to 400 percent. They have a couple of tariffs at 400 percent. Nobody knows that. Nobody talks about that.

Q. Mr. President, Canada is America's second largest trading partner. Are there any plans for renewed trade talks between the U.S. and Canada? And has there been any decline in terms of Canadian tourism to the U.S.? And perhaps you folks would know that.
The President. Well, I don't know. I can tell you this. You know, Canada has been ripping off the United States for many, many years—for decades, many decades. We lost anywhere from
$60- to $100 billion with Canada. We traditionally lose that for last 15 years.
It's a very unfair deal. They charge tremendous tariffs to our farmers. They take advantage of our farmers. They take advantage of our tourists. They take advantage of airlines.

Something that nobody brought up. I'll bring it up right now. They think it's so sensitive, but I don't find it sensitive. Canada has all of its major banks here, and we're their biggest source of income, far bigger than they are in Canada. They basically don't allow banks of America to be in Canada. That's sort of emblematic of the way they treat us.

Think of it. So they have their banks here—Bank of Canada, all of the big banks—big, beautiful banks. I think they have six or seven major banks here. We don't have our banks there. You know why? They don't allow it.

I had a case about a week ago where a friend of mine was buying a Gulfstream jet, and he said: "You know, it's a crazy thing. We're not able—that Canada won't certify Gulfstream." Won't certify it. Gulfstream is the best private jet. You know, considered the best of the best, and they won't certify it in Canada because they make a competitor: Bombardier Global Express.
And so their competitor didn't want them to have competition. So, for approximately 9 years, this has been going on. They won't certify Gulfstream.

So he's very friendly with Gulfstream. He told the head of Gulfstream to call me. Gave him the numbers. We called. We spoke. He said: "Sir, I've spent $60 million trying to get certified in Canada. I can't get certified in Canada. They won't do it."
So I immediately said I'm putting a major tariff on Bombardier and other things that they sent until they're certified. They got certified in 2 hours. [Laughter]

I got a call from the Prime Minister, "President, what seems to be the problem?" I said: "Well, you have a little problem. For 9 years, you didn't certify Gulfstream." Essentially, they can't sell any plane in anything having to do with Canada. But Bombardier has free rein over the United States. Both good planes. Very good planes.

And I said, "So what we're going to do is, we're going to charge you tariffs on various products, including Bombardier." We put a nice, big—and within 30 minutes, I guess it took—maybe less—everything got certified.
He told me they spent millions and millions of dollars on legal fees over about a 9-year period trying to do it. I did it in a matter of moments.

But that's the way they treat us. And I thought that was really egregious. It was incredible, because everyone knows how good the Gulfstream is. It's a—it's the best plane, and for them to not be allowed to sell it in Canada—but that's the way they are.

And people are surprised when I say it. Like, I have China coming here. A lot of people say: "Who's the toughest one to deal with? Is it China, sir? Is it China? Is it Vietnam? Is it"—I said, "No, actually, it's Canada." Canada has felt emboldened. We—they had Presidents that didn't know what was happening. Not only the last one, all of them. I mean, they just were taken into—our country's been taken advantage of by Canada.

They took 20 percent of our car industry out. I don't blame them for that, but if we would have had a President that knew what was happening, nobody would have left. Now they're all coming back. All they would have had to do is charge tariffs, and they would have put tariffs on. If you build a car in Canada, you have to pay a 25-percent tariff, and nobody could pay. And if that didn't work, you make it 50 percent, or if that didn't work, you make it 100 percent.

And we have everybody coming. Or you stop doing business with the nation. You know, when we lose $60- to $100 billion with Canada, I could say, "Well, if we don't do business"—because we don't need—we have more oil and gas than they do. We have tremendous forests. We don't need their lumber. We don't need the things they have. They need what we have. They do most of their business with us. I've heard numbers—95 percent. We do a very small percentage compared to others. We do a very small percentage by comparison to that.

But they need us. We don't need them. They've taken advantage of us for years, and it's time to stop. We can't lose $60- to $100 billion a year for the privilege of allowing them to make cars. We don't want their cars. We want the cars to be made in Detroit and in South Carolina and in Tennessee and in all of our places where we make cars. We don't want them to be made in Canada. So this is nothing against anybody.

And this started with Trudeau. Trudeau and I used to have it out pretty good, and now we have this new guy, who's a nice guy, but you know, he's just—and then they have the other guy, the slob. I guess some people call him a slob. I don't want to call him that because I want to be nice.

But—and I did change the name of a certain lake to Lake America, just like I changed the name of the Gulf of America—of—Mexico to Gulf of America. And people in this country love it. You know, we have 92 percent of the frontage, and why was it Gulf of Mexico? We have most of the frontage, almost all—93, 94 percent.
So we do things like that because we're fighting for our country.
Canada has taken advantage of us. They have ripped us off for years, and now we're turning the tables very—very easily turning the tables.
Yes.
